extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of theatre/dramatic criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and standards for judging dramatic roles, performances, and professional conduct of actors as discussed in a 19th-century theatrical biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's moral/educational function
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama, to be true to its full function, must sometimes teach terrible lessons terribly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages argue that chronic political and social experience is often terrible, and the drama must at times present those truths in powerful, even horrific form (example: the depiction of Cade and the peasants). The text defends such portrayals as part of drama's function to reflect retributive justice and the truths of history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge impersonation by truth and power in its own kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic impersonation should be judged from its truth and power in its own kind and range, not from negative comparisons to other aesthetic or ethical types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic states that judgment based on what a role is not (its aesthetic or ethical inferiority to other characters) is incorrect; the player 'professes to exhibit' only a certain kind, and evaluation should be internal to that kind and range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of character over aesthetic prettiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters representing raw, strong impulses (barbaric manhood, passions of revenge, etc.) are valid and may be more noble or wholesome than cultivated, conventional types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text defends representations whose energies 'spurn hypocrisy and mean compromises' and whose passions 'flame straight to their marks.' It acknowledges such portrayals will offend some, but argues they can be ennobling and truthful rather than merely vulgar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral justification of violent or vengeful portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal of vengeance or harsh justice can have moral justification if presented as Nemesis or retributive justice rather than capricious assassination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cade is described as 'never the assassin, but always the judge' — his vengeance 'never the blow of caprice, but always of Nemesis.' The author argues such roles can teach rather than incite vengeance, and the blame for any ferocity taken from a performance lies with the spectator rather than the player.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance should be carefully studied and conscientious
rubrics_metrics.description: A great performance is not mere empty histrionics but a carefully-studied and conscientious condensation of a whole life into the stage time available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises Forrest's three-hour condensation of a vigorous life, noting the importance of study and conscientious shaping rather than strutting or superficial display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's public conduct and defense of personal character
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor's personal honour and public character are of primary importance and may justify direct public rebuttal of slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Forrest addresses his audience to vindicate himself from newspaper libel, asserting he values his character 'far higher than all the fame' ever acquired by actors. The narrative treats such public vindication as legitimate and praiseworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional autonomy regarding charitable performances
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor has the right to control the disposal of his professional services and may set a rule limiting charity performances to avoid exploitation and favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest explains he makes a rule to perform for charity only for the Theatrical Fund for decayed actors, because otherwise he would be obliged to offend by choosing among many calls and waste his livelihood. He challenges anonymous philanthropic critics to match his monetary generosity if they insist he perform gratis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge art by audience misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: If an exhibition of art 'feeds class-hatred or personal ferocity' the fault lies with the spectator, not the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts the moral result of portraying condign punishment is to dissuade wrongdoing; if viewers misuse it to incite hatred, blame lies with them. ('If in any instance its exhibition fed class-hatred... the blame lay with the spectator, not with the player.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning dramatic expression from real-life models
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors can learn powerful dramatic expression by observing real persons' spontaneous transformations and gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest's anecdote of observing General Jackson's sudden change from drooping decrepitude to 'sublime power' is cited as an 'unintentional lesson' in dramatic expression that informed his modeling of explosive stage moments (e.g., Richelieu).
